text:
“I could not put it back on without hooks,” said Lucien, blushing.

“Bérénice will go and fetch some; they will not be superfluous here,” said the tradesman with a horribly mocking air.

“Papa Camusot,” said Coralie, casting him a look filled with atrocious contempt, “have the courage of your cowardice! Come, say everything you are thinking. You think monsieur’s boots look like mine? I forbid you to take off your boots,” she said to Lucien. “Yes, Monsieur Camusot, yes, those boots are exactly the same as the ones that stood with their arms crossed before my hearth the other day, while monsieur, hidden in my dressing room, was waiting for them; he had spent the night here. That is what you think, eh? Think it; I want you to. It is the plain truth. I am deceiving you. And then? It pleases me!”

She sat down without anger and with the most unconstrained air in the world, looking at Camusot and Lucien, who did not dare look at each other.

“I shall believe only what you wish me to believe,” said Camusot. “Do not jest; I am in the wrong.”

“Either I am a shameless wanton who, in a single moment, has become infatuated with monsieur, or I am a poor, wretched creature who has felt for the first time the true love after which all women run. In either case, you must leave me or take me as I am,” she said, making a sovereign gesture by which she crushed the merchant.

“Can it be true?” said Camusot, who saw from Lucien’s bearing that Coralie was not joking and who was begging to be deceived.

“I love mademoiselle,” said Lucien.

On hearing those words spoken in an emotional voice, Coralie flung herself upon her poet’s neck, clasped him in her arms, and turned her head toward the silk merchant, showing him the admirable tableau of love that she formed with Lucien.

“Poor Musot, take back everything you have given me; I want nothing from you. I love this boy madly, not for his wit, but for his beauty. I prefer poverty with him to millions with you.”

Camusot sank into an armchair, put his head in his hands, and remained silent.

“Would you like us to go away?” she asked him with incredible ferocity.

A chill ran down Lucien’s back when he saw himself burdened with a woman, an actress, and a household.

“Stay here, keep everything, Coralie,” said the tradesman in a faint, sorrowful voice that came from his soul. “I do not want to take anything back. There are, however, sixty thousand francs’ worth of furnishings here, but I could not reconcile myself to the thought of my Coralie in poverty. And yet, before long, you will be in poverty. However great monsieur’s talents may be, they cannot provide you with a living. That is what awaits all of us old men! Leave me, Coralie, the right to come and see you sometimes: I can be useful to you. Besides, I confess it, it would be impossible for me to live without you.”

The gentleness of this poor man, dispossessed of all his happiness at the moment when he believed himself happiest, deeply touched Lucien, but not Coralie.

“Come, my poor Musot, come as often as you like,” she said. “I shall love you better when I am no longer deceiving you.”

Camusot appeared content not to be driven from his earthly paradise, where he would doubtless suffer, but where he hoped later to regain all his rights, trusting to the hazards of Parisian life and to the temptations that were going to surround Lucien. The crafty old merchant thought that sooner or later this handsome young man would permit himself some infidelities, and in order to spy on him, to ruin him in Coralie’s estimation, he wished to remain their friend. This cowardice of true passion frightened Lucien. Camusot offered to give them dinner at Véry’s in the Palais-Royal, and the offer was accepted.

“What happiness!” cried Coralie when Camusot had gone. “No more garret in the Latin Quarter; you will live here, we shall never part, and, to keep up appearances, you will take a small apartment in the rue Charlot—and let the ship sail where it may!”

She began to dance her Spanish step with a vigor that expressed an indomitable passion.

“I can earn five hundred francs a month by working hard,” said Lucien.

“I have just as much at the theater, not counting the performance fees. Camusot will always provide my clothes; he loves me! With fifteen hundred francs a month, we shall live like Croesuses.”

“And the horses, and the coachman, and the servant?” said Bérénice.

“I shall run into debt,” cried Coralie.

She began dancing a jig with Lucien.

“Then I must accept Finot’s proposals,” cried Lucien.

“Come,” said Coralie, “I shall dress and take you to your newspaper; I shall wait for you in the carriage on the boulevard.”

Lucien sat down on a sofa, watched the actress dress, and gave himself up to the gravest reflections. He would have preferred to leave Coralie free rather than be thrust into the obligations of such a marriage; but he saw her so beautiful, so well formed, so alluring, that he was seized by the picturesque aspects of this Bohemian life and threw down the gauntlet in Fortune’s face. Bérénice was ordered to oversee Lucien’s move and installation. Then Coralie—triumphant, beautiful, happy—carried off her beloved lover, her poet, and crossed all Paris to go to the rue Saint-Fiacre. Lucien ran lightly up the stairs and presented himself as a master in the newspaper’s offices. Coloquinte, still with his stamped paper on his head, and old Giroudeau again told him, with a fair degree of hypocrisy, that no one had come.

“But the editors must meet somewhere to agree on the contents of the newspaper,” he said.

“Probably, but the editorial staff is no concern of mine,” said the captain of the Imperial Guard, who went back to checking his wrappers while making his eternal “Brrum! Brrum!”

At that moment, by a chance that one must call fortunate or unfortunate, Finot came to tell Giroudeau of his sham abdication and to commend his interests to his care.

“No diplomacy with monsieur; he is on the newspaper,” Finot said to his uncle, taking Lucien’s hand and shaking it.

“Ah! Monsieur is on the newspaper,” cried Giroudeau, surprised by his nephew’s gesture. “Well, monsieur, you did not have much trouble getting onto it.”
